body.text: Emilie Miller was 12 when she suffered a spinal cord injury that left her a quadriplegic.
Unable to carry her own baby, she and her husband David were exploring other ways to start a family when her cousin approached them with a life-changing offer.
She would be their surrogate.
"It's such an overwhelming, massive thing for someone to offer to do for you," Ms Miller recalled.
Three years later, they are now parents to seven-month-old Max.
While it has been a lengthy and difficult journey to parenthood, they know they are luckier than many to have found a surrogate on home soil.
"For other couples, that's not always the experience,"
Report recommends more accessible surrogacy
About 80 per cent of Australians' surrogacy arrangements happen outside the country.
The Australian Law Reform Commission (ALRC) said this was because there were numerous barriers to accessing surrogacy domestically.
"The problems in our domestic laws are driving intended parents overseas where the exploitation and the harms are greatest," ALRC Justice Mordy Bromberg said.
The ALRC recommended sweeping changes in its final report to address the issue.
They included the introduction of a nationally consistent surrogacy framework overseen by a regulator to streamline the current "patchwork" of state and territory laws.
The report also proposed entitling surrogates to greater financial compensation for the impacts of pregnancy and childbirth, so they were not left financially disadvantaged.
However, the ALRC stopped short of lifting Australia's ban on commercial surrogacy.
Australia only allows an "altruistic" model, meaning surrogates can be reimbursed for certain expenses but cannot be paid a reward or fee.
"We don't want to see the commodification of the baby. We don't want to allow a payment in exchange for the baby," Justice Bromberg said.
"Secondly, we don't want financial inducements, inducing surrogates into an activity that ultimately will harm them. That might compromise their free and informed consent."
'Needle in a haystack'
A person's postcode has a big impact on what is allowed when it comes to surrogacy in Australia.
For instance, in South Australia, people must complete a police check before they proceed with surrogacy, but that is not required elsewhere.
Victoria and Tasmania legislate that a surrogate must previously have given birth, which is also not required elsewhere.
"We have eight systems," surrogacy lawyer and dad through surrogacy, Stephen Page, said.
There are also tight restrictions on advertising, making it tough for people to find surrogates through social media.
It means only about 20 per cent of surrogacy arrangements in Australia are between strangers.
"We're talking about a needle in a haystack,"
Surrogate weighs in on proposed changes
Gold Coast mum Roxanne Brewer was one such rare case, deciding to become a surrogate for strangers in 2019.
Money was not front of mind when she offered to help Matt and Wilson, a gay couple she met online.
However, she said the expanded compensation suggested by the ALRC may encourage more women to explore surrogacy as she did.
"As long as the ethics around a woman's rights are protected, I think it's OK,"
The ALRC has also recommended intended parents be recognised as legal parents from birth, a proposal close to Ms Miller's heart.
"Max is seven months old, and we've only just been granted parentage of our own baby, which is wild," she said.
"But that's just the legal process that exists around surrogacy cases in Australia at the moment."
Opposition to surrogacy law expansion
Not everyone agrees surrogacy laws should be expanded.
In submissions to the ALRC's inquiry, multiple religious groups said separating a child from its gestational mother violated its rights to biological and emotional bonds.
The Australian Christian Lobby has criticised the ALRC report and urged all governments to reject its key recommendations.

"While the commission's report does not explicitly recommend commercial surrogacy in Australia, when read closely, the report's recommendations take Australia most of the way there," chief executive Michelle Pearse said in a statement.
Justice Bromberg said the ALRC had endeavoured to take all perspectives into account when preparing the report.
"Surrogacy can be a social good. It can also involve harm and exploitation," he said.
"A balance needs to be struck so that we can have the good and avoid the bad."
The Australian Catholic Bishops Conference has previously called for a complete national ban on all forms of surrogacy, saying it "turns pregnancy into a transaction".
But family creation lawyer Sarah Jefford said banning surrogacy would only take it underground, saying better accessibility in Australia was the answer.
"We've got the best medical systems; we could have the best legal protections for everybody," she said.
"[We can] ensure the surrogate can exercise her bodily autonomy and access good health care and that the baby's rights are also protected."
The federal government said it would consider the ALRC's recommendations alongside the states and territories.
